title: Queues
definition: A queue is a linear data structure that follows the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principle. Elements are added at one end (rear) and removed from the other end (front).
conceptExplanation: The FIFO principle means the first element enqueued is the first one to be dequeued. The two primary operations are enqueue (add to rear) and dequeue (remove from front). Front points to the front element, Rear points to the rear element.
keyPoints: - FIFO principle - Operations at two ends (front and rear) - Enqueue, Dequeue operations - Array or linked implementation
importantTerminology: Queue, Front, Rear, Enqueue, Dequeue, Underflow, Overflow, FIFO
workingPrinciple: Enqueue adds an element to the rear of the queue, incrementing the rear pointer. Dequeue removes the front element, incrementing the front pointer. If enqueue is attempted on a full queue, it causes overflow. If dequeue is attempted on an empty queue, it causes underflow.
realLifeExample: Print job queue, customer service line, breadth-first search, task scheduling
dsaExample: Implementing BFS, task scheduling, print queue management
diagram: Queue operations showing enqueue and dequeue: front -> [10] -> [20] -> [30] -> rear (front moves on dequeue, rear moves on enqueue)
algorithm:
Enqueue Operation:
1. Check if queue is full (overflow)
2. If not, increment rear pointer
3. Add element at rear position
4. Return success

Dequeue Operation:
1. Check if queue is empty (underflow)
2. If not, get element at front
3. Increment front pointer
4. Return removed element

Front Operation:
1. Check if queue is empty
2. Return element at front position without removing it

Rear Operation:
1. Check if queue is empty
2. Return element at rear position without removing it
pseudocode:
BEGIN
  // Enqueue
  IF queue IS full
    PRINT 'Overflow'
  ELSE
    SET rear = rear + 1
    SET queue[rear] = item
  END IF

  // Dequeue
  IF queue IS empty
    PRINT 'Underflow'
  ELSE
    SET item = queue[front]
    SET front = front + 1
  END IF

  // Front operation
  IF queue IS empty
    PRINT 'Queue is empty'
  ELSE
    PRINT 'Front element:', queue[front]
  END IF

  // Rear operation
  IF queue IS empty
    PRINT 'Queue is empty'
  ELSE
    PRINT 'Rear element:', queue[rear]
  END IF
END
complexity: Time: Enqueue O(1), Dequeue O(1), Front/Rear O(1)\nSpace: O(n) for n elements (capacity limited)
applications: Print job queue, customer service BFS, task scheduling, breadth-first search
advantages: O(1) enqueue/dequeue, fair processing order (FIFO), useful for resource scheduling
limitations: Fixed size (array-based), not suitable for LIFO requirements, circular queue needed for efficient space usage
commonMistakes: Confusing enqueue/dequeue with stack operations (push/pop), not checking overflow/underflow, front/rear index off-by-one errors
importantExamPoints:

Array vs linked implementation

fiveMarkQuestions.question: Explain queue operations, implementations, and applications.
fiveMarkQuestions.answer:
A queue follows FIFO (First-In-First-Out) principle. Elements are added at rear and removed from front. Operations: - Enqueue: Adds element to rear. Time: O(1). - Dequeue: Removes element from front. Time: O(1). - Front: Returns front element without removal. - Rear: Returns rear element. - isEmpty: Checks if queue empty. - isFull: Checks if capacity reached.

Array Implementation: Fixed capacity, front and rear indices. Circular queue wraps around when reaching end, reusing space. Time: O(1) for all operations.

Linked Implementation: Dynamic size using linked list. Front points to first node, rear points to last node. No fixed capacity, no overflow.

Applications: Print job scheduling (first job printed first), customer service lines, task scheduling in OS, breadth-first search in graphs, event simulation.

Circular Queue: Overcomes array limitation by wrapping rear to beginning when reaching end. Condition: (rear + 1) % capacity == front for full. Efficient space utilization.

tenMarkQuestions.question: Explain queue with array and linked implementations, circular queue, and applications.
tenMarkQuestions.answer:
A queue follows FIFO principle. 

Array Implementation: Fixed-size array with front and rear indices. Enqueue: rear = (rear + 1) % capacity, store element. Dequeue: item = queue[front], front = (front + 1) % capacity. Circular queue efficiently reuses space.

Linked Implementation: Using linked list with front and rear pointers. Dynamic size, no overflow. Enqueue: create new node, attach at rear, update rear. Dequeue: move front to next node.

Circular Queue: Solves wastage in linear array. Uses modulo arithmetic. Full condition: (rear + 1) % capacity == front. Empty condition: front == rear.

Applications: 1) Print spooling - jobs queued in order. 2) CPU scheduling - round-robin uses queue. 3) Breadth-first search - visits nodes level by level. 4) Customer service - first-come-first-served. 5) Task scheduling in operating systems.

Complexity: All operations O(1). Space: O(n) for n elements.
